title: 🌍 UNIT 1: MAJOR GEOLOGICAL PROCESSES ASSOCIATED WITH PLATE TECTONICS
notes: Earth is a dynamic planet whose surface is continuously changed by internal and external forces.

title: 🧩 1.1 CONTINENTAL DRIFT THEORY
notes:
Continental Drift Theory states that the Earth's continents have moved relative to one another over geological time.

🔹 Alfred Wegener → German meteorologist who proposed the theory in 1912.

🔹 Pangaea → ancient supercontinent containing most of the Earth's continental landmasses.

🔹 Laurasia → northern part of Pangaea.

🔹 Gondwanaland → southern part of Pangaea.

⭐ Pangaea gradually broke apart, and the continents drifted to their present positions over millions of years.

title: 🧭 1.1.1 GEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE FOR CONTINENTAL DRIFT
notes:
Wegener supported continental drift using several types of evidence:

1️⃣ Coastline similarity → Africa and South America fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle.

2️⃣ Rock type and structure → similar rocks of the same age and mountain belts occur on different continents.

3️⃣ Fossil evidence → identical fossils occur on continents now separated by oceans.

🔹 Mesosaurus fossils → found in both South America and Africa.

4️⃣ Paleoclimatic evidence → reconstructed ancient climates show similarities between continents now far apart.

⭐ These similarities suggest that the continents were once joined.

title: ⚠️ 1.1.2 WHY WAS WEGENER'S THEORY NOT EASILY ACCEPTED?
notes:
The scientific community initially rejected Wegener's theory because:

🔹 Wegener was not a geologist by profession.

🔹 Much of the important supporting data came from the Southern Hemisphere, while many influential geoscientists were based in the Northern Hemisphere.

🔹 Scientists considered the proposed timing of continental movement difficult to accept.

🔹 There was no convincing direct evidence explaining how continents could move.

⭐ Wegener's major contribution → introduced the idea that continents are laterally mobile rather than permanently fixed.

title: 🌐 1.2 PLATE TECTONICS THEORY
notes:
Plate tectonics explains the movement and deformation of Earth's outer layers.

🔹 Lithosphere → Earth's crust and uppermost mantle; it is divided into large and small plates.

🔹 Asthenosphere → ductile layer beneath the lithosphere over which plates move.

🔹 Plates → large pieces of lithosphere that move slowly, generally a few centimeters per year.

⭐ Plates may contain continental crust, oceanic crust, or both.

The theory provides a framework for explaining mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes, fossils and the ages of rocks.

title: 🪨 1.2.1 CONTINENTAL & OCEANIC CRUST
notes:
The interaction of plates depends partly on the type of crust involved.

🔹 Continental crust → largely granitic and less dense.

🔹 Oceanic crust → largely basaltic and denser.

⭐ Because oceanic crust is denser, it can be forced beneath less-dense crust at convergent boundaries.

title: 🔄 1.3 PLATE MOVEMENTS & PLATE BOUNDARIES
notes:
Plates interact mainly in three ways:

1️⃣ Convergent → plates move toward each other.

2️⃣ Divergent → plates move away from each other.

3️⃣ Transform → plates slide laterally past each other.

⭐ Boundary names:
Convergent = Destructive
Divergent = Constructive
Transform = Conservative.

title: 💥 1.3.1 CONVERGENT PLATE BOUNDARY
notes:
At a convergent boundary, two plates move toward each other.

🔹 When a denser plate meets a less-dense plate → the denser plate may be subducted beneath the other.

🔹 Oceanic + continental → oceanic plate subducts, producing magma and volcanic activity.

🔹 Example → Nazca Plate subducting beneath the South American Plate contributes to the formation of the Andes volcanoes.

🔹 Oceanic + oceanic → one plate may subduct beneath the other and form a volcanic island arc.

🔹 Example → Mariana Islands.

🔹 Continental + continental → collision compresses and uplifts the crust.

🔹 Example → Indo-Australian Plate + Eurasian Plate → Himalayas.

⭐ Convergence can produce subduction, volcanoes, earthquakes and mountain building.

title: 🌊 1.3.2 DIVERGENT PLATE BOUNDARY
notes:
At a divergent boundary, plates move away from each other.

🔹 Rising magma reaches the surface and forms new oceanic crust.

🔹 Seafloor spreading → new seafloor forms at oceanic ridges and pushes plates apart.

🔹 Mid-Atlantic Ridge → major example of oceanic divergence.

🔹 Shallow earthquakes and undersea volcanic activity are common.

🔹 Continental divergence → produces fractures and rift valleys.

🔹 East African Rift Valley → important example.

⭐ Continued continental separation may eventually lead to the formation of a new ocean.

title: ↔️ 1.3.3 TRANSFORM FAULT BOUNDARY
notes:
A transform boundary occurs where two plates slide horizontally past one another along fractures.

🔹 Crust → neither created nor destroyed.

🔹 Plates may stick because of friction and later suddenly slip.

🔹 Sudden slipping → earthquakes.

🔹 Example → San Andreas Fault in California.

⭐ Transform = lateral movement + earthquakes + no creation or destruction of crust.

title: 🔥 1.3.4 FORCES RESPONSIBLE FOR PLATE MOVEMENT
notes:
Plate movement is ultimately related to the Earth's internal energy.

🔹 Convection currents → movement of heated material in the mantle/asthenosphere.

🔥 Rising currents → carry heat toward the surface, especially beneath oceanic ridges.

⬇️ Descending currents → sink at subduction zones after losing heat.

⭐ The moving asthenosphere helps drive the rigid lithospheric plates above it.

title: 🌋 1.4 MAJOR GEOLOGICAL PROCESSES
notes:
Geological processes are natural forces that shape the physical structure of the Earth.

They are broadly divided into:

🔴 Endogenic forces → originate inside the Earth.

🔵 Exogenic forces → originate outside the Earth or act from the Earth's exterior.

⭐ Endogenic → build, deform and uplift the surface.

⭐ Exogenic → mainly wear down, transport and deposit materials.

title: 🔴 1.4.1 INTERNAL (ENDOGENIC) FORCES
notes:
Endogenic forces originate inside the Earth and create irregularities and unevenness on the crust.

Major processes include:

🔹 Folding
🔹 Faulting
🔹 Earthquakes
🔹 Volcanic eruptions

⭐ These forces can produce mountains, rift valleys, block mountains and volcanic landforms.

title: ⛰️ 1.4.1.1 FOLDING
notes:
Folding occurs when rock layers are compressed and bent by earth movements.

🔺 Anticline → upward bend or upfold.

🔻 Syncline → downward bend or downfold.

Other folds produced by increasing compression:

🔹 Asymmetrical fold → one limb is steeper than the other.

🔹 Over fold → one limb is pushed over the other.

🔹 Overthrust fold → intense pressure causes fracturing and one limb is pushed forward over the other.

⭐ Folding is an important process in the formation of fold mountains.

title: 🏔️ 1.4.1.2 TYPES OF FOLD MOUNTAINS
notes:
Fold mountains are grouped into:

1️⃣ Young fold mountains → formed during relatively recent mountain-building periods; generally high and prominent.

Examples → Andes, Rockies, Alps, Himalayas, Atlas and Australian Alps.

2️⃣ Old fold mountains → formed during older mountain-building periods; generally lower and more weathered.

Examples → Scandinavian Mountains, Appalachian Mountains and Urals.

⭐ Mountain building process → Orogenesis.

title: 🪨 1.4.1.3 FAULTING
notes:
A fault is a crack or fracture in the Earth's crust along which rocks are displaced.

🔹 Main forces involved → tension and compression.

When parallel faults develop, the land between them may:

⬇️ Sink → Rift valley / Graben.

⬆️ Rise → Block mountain / Horst.

🔹 East African Rift Valley → example of a rift valley.

🔹 Afar Horst → example of a block mountain.

title: 🌎 1.4.1.4 EARTHQUAKES
notes:
An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement of rocks beneath the Earth's surface.

🔹 Rapid release of stored strain energy → seismic waves.

🔹 Faults → major locations of earthquake activity.

🔹 Seismograph → instrument used to detect and record earthquake waves.

🔹 Richter scale → scale used in the textbook to express earthquake magnitude from 0 to 9.

⭐ Most major earthquakes are associated with tectonic plate boundaries and faults.

title: 📡 1.4.1.5 SEISMIC WAVES
notes:
Earthquake waves are broadly divided into body waves and surface waves.

🔹 P waves → primary body waves; compress and expand rocks in the direction of travel and arrive first.

🔹 S waves → secondary body waves; vibrate at right angles to their direction of travel.

🔹 Surface waves → travel along the Earth's surface and generally cause the most destructive shaking.

🔹 Love waves + Rayleigh waves → major types of surface waves.

⭐ Focus → point where the earthquake originates.
⭐ Epicenter → point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.

title: 🌊 1.4.1.6 EFFECTS & OCCURRENCE OF EARTHQUAKES
notes:
Earthquakes may cause:

🔹 Ground deformation
🔹 Landslides
🔹 Mudflows
🔹 Changes in groundwater flow
🔹 Damage to buildings, bridges, pipelines, railways and dams
🔹 Fires
🔹 Tsunamis

🌊 Underwater earthquakes can generate tsunamis by violently disturbing the seafloor.

🌍 Major earthquake belts include:

🔹 Circum-Pacific Belt / Ring of Fire → accounts for about 80% of earthquake energy in the textbook.

🔹 Mediterranean-Asian Belt → accounts for about 15%.

🔹 Other seismic belts → include mid-oceanic ridges and the Great Rift Valley of East Africa.

title: 🌋 1.4.1.7 VOLCANISM
notes:
Volcanism is the process through which molten rock, gases and solid materials are forced toward or onto the Earth's surface.

🔹 Magma → molten rock beneath the Earth's surface.

🔹 Lava → magma that reaches the Earth's surface.

🔹 Vent → pipe-like opening through which magma erupts.

🔹 Fissure → large, narrow crack through which magma can rise and spread.

⭐ Vent eruption → commonly builds a volcanic cone.
⭐ Fissure eruption → can produce extensive lava plateaus.

title: 🌋 1.4.1.8 VOLCANOES & THEIR OCCURRENCE
notes:
Volcano → usually a cone-shaped structure formed by accumulated erupted materials.

Volcanoes occur mainly near plate boundaries:

🔹 Divergent boundaries → volcanic activity associated with tension and rising magma.

🔹 Convergent boundaries → volcanic activity associated with compression and subduction.

🔹 Oceanic ridges → chains of oceanic volcanoes.

🔹 East African Rift Valley → important region of volcanic activity.

⭐ Nearly 90% of the world's active or historically active volcanoes are situated around the Pacific Ring of Fire, according to the textbook.

title: 🇪🇹 1.4.1.9 VOLCANO TYPES BY ACTIVITY
notes:
1️⃣ Extinct volcano → not erupting and not expected to erupt again.

🔹 Example → Mount Zuqualla, Ethiopia.

2️⃣ Dormant volcano → currently inactive but has erupted in historic times and may erupt again.

🔹 Example → Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania.

3️⃣ Active volcano → has erupted or is thought to have erupted during the last 500 years.

🔹 Example → Erta Ale, Ethiopia.

title: 🌋 1.4.1.10 TYPES OF VOLCANOES
notes:
🔹 Shield volcano → broad, low profile; formed mainly by fluid lava flows that spread widely.

🔹 Stratovolcano → steep cone made of alternating layers of lava and pyroclastic materials; often associated with explosive eruptions.

🔹 Cinder cone → conical hill mainly composed of cinder-sized pyroclastic materials.

🔹 Crater → depression formed by volcanic collapse, violent explosion or later erosion.

🔹 Caldera → large basin-shaped depression commonly formed when a magma chamber drains and the overlying volcanic structure collapses.

title: 🪨 1.4.1.11 INTRUSIVE VOLCANIC LANDFORMS
notes:
When magma cools and solidifies beneath the Earth's surface, intrusive or plutonic igneous rocks and landforms are formed.

🔹 Batholith → very large, deep intrusion that may form the core of a mountain.

🔹 Sill → near-horizontal sheet of igneous rock between rock layers.

🔹 Dyke → near-vertical sheet formed when magma rises through a crack and solidifies.

⭐ Intrusive → forms below the Earth's surface.

title: 🔵 1.4.2 EXTERNAL (EXOGENIC) FORCES
notes:
Exogenic forces act on the Earth's surface from outside.

Major agents include:

💧 Running water
💨 Wind
🌊 Sea waves
❄️ Moving ice

External forces generally reduce surface irregularities through:

1️⃣ Denudation → lowering of land by wearing away the surface.

2️⃣ Deposition → accumulation of transported materials.

title: 🪨 1.4.2.1 WEATHERING
notes:
Weathering is the gradual breakdown of rocks at or near the Earth's surface.

Two main types:

1️⃣ Physical / Mechanical weathering → rocks break into smaller pieces without changing their chemical characteristics.

2️⃣ Chemical weathering → minerals undergo changes in the internal structure of rocks.

⭐ Weathering breaks rocks down; erosion transports the resulting materials.

title: 🌡️ 1.4.2.2 PHYSICAL WEATHERING
notes:
Major physical weathering processes include:

🔹 Thermal expansion and contraction → repeated heating and cooling cause rock layers to expand and contract.

🔹 Exfoliation → outer rock layers peel away, especially in hot and dry areas.

🔹 Frost action → water freezes in rock cracks, expands and widens the cracks.

🔹 Plant and animal action → roots grow into cracks while animals disturb and break materials.

⭐ Physical weathering changes the size of rocks without fundamentally changing their chemical composition.

title: 🧪 1.4.2.3 CHEMICAL WEATHERING
notes:
Chemical weathering changes the internal chemical structure of rocks.

💧 Rainwater is an important agent because it can contain dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide.

🔹 Solution → acidic rainwater dissolves soluble rock materials.

🔹 Carbonation → carbonic acid in rainwater reacts with carbonate rocks such as limestone.

🔹 Hydrolysis → acidic water breaks down minerals and produces clay and soluble salts.

🌿 Plants and microorganisms also contribute through mineral absorption and organic acids from decaying vegetation.

title: 🕳️ 1.4.2.4 LIMESTONE LANDFORMS
notes:
Chemical weathering is especially important in limestone areas.

🔹 Rainwater dissolves limestone and gradually enlarges underground openings.

🔹 Caves → large underground openings formed by dissolution.

🇪🇹 Sof Omar Cave → important Ethiopian example.

🔹 Stalactite → limestone deposit hanging downward from a cave ceiling.

🔹 Stalagmite → limestone deposit growing upward from the cave floor.

🔹 Pillar → forms when a stalactite and stalagmite join.

title: 🌊 1.4.2.5 EROSION & DEPOSITION
notes:
Soil erosion → movement of soil and rock particles from one place to another.

Major agents:

💧 Running water
💧 Underground water
💨 Wind
🌊 Sea waves
❄️ Glaciers

⭐ Running water is one of the most powerful agents shaping the Earth's surface.

🔹 Faster water and steeper slopes → generally greater erosive power.
🔹 Vegetation cover → reduces erosion by protecting the soil.

title: 💧 1.4.2.6 RUNNING WATER EROSION
notes:
Runoff erosion produces several forms:

🔹 Sheet erosion → surface water removes a thin, relatively even layer of topsoil.

🔹 Rill erosion → water cuts small channels or ditches into the soil.

🔹 Gully erosion → channels become wider and deeper, often becoming severe where vegetation has been removed.

⭐ Sheet → Rill → Gully = increasing concentration and depth of runoff channels.

title: 🏞️ 1.4.2.7 RIVER LANDFORMS
notes:
🌄 Upper course → river is swift and erosive.

🔹 V-shaped valley → narrow, steep-sided valley shaped like V.

🔹 Gorge → deep, narrow valley with steep or nearly vertical walls.

🔹 Waterfall → forms where resistant rock remains while softer rock is eroded faster.

🔹 Interlocking spurs → ridges of land projecting into the river valley.

🔹 Rapids → fast, turbulent sections of a river with a relatively steep gradient.

🌿 Middle course → valley becomes wider as tributaries increase the river's volume.

🔹 Confluence → point where a tributary joins the main river.

title: 〰️ 1.4.2.8 MIDDLE & LOWER COURSE LANDFORMS
notes:
🔹 Meander → winding or zigzag course of a river caused by erosion and deposition.

🔹 Ox-bow lake → crescent-shaped lake formed from a cut-off abandoned meander.

🔹 Flood plain → low, flat land formed by deposition of sediments along a river, especially in its lower course.

🔹 Delta → generally triangular deposit of sediment at a river mouth.

⭐ Upper course → mainly erosion.
⭐ Lower course → slower flow + greater deposition.

title: 💨 1.4.2.9 WIND ACTION
notes:
Wind is a powerful geomorphic agent, especially in desert and semi-desert regions.

🔹 Sand dunes → hills of sand formed when wind deposits sand around obstacles.

🔹 Barkhan → crescent-shaped sand dune.

🔹 Loess deposits → wind-deposited fine materials that can form fertile soils.

⭐ North China → noted in the textbook for large loess deposits.

title: 🌊 1.4.2.10 WORK OF THE SEA
notes:
Sea waves perform both erosion and deposition along coastlines.

🔹 Beach → strip of coastal land covered by sediments.

🔹 Spit → narrow deposit of sand or silt attached to the land at one end and extending into the sea.

🔹 Lagoon → saltwater area separated from the sea by loose sand banks.

⭐ Coastal landforms result from the combined action of marine erosion and deposition.

title: ⬇️ 1.4.2.11 MASS WASTING
notes:
Mass wasting → downslope movement of rock, regolith and soil mainly under the influence of gravity.

Major controlling factors:

🔹 Gravity → primary controlling force.
🔹 Water → reduces cohesion between particles and can trigger movement.
🔹 Slope angle → steeper slopes are generally more unstable.
🔹 Human activities → farming and overgrazing can increase instability.

🇪🇹 Mass wasting has occurred in different parts of Ethiopia and can destroy lives and property.

title: 🧠 UNIT 1 KEY DIFFERENCES
notes:
🔄 Continental Drift → continents move relative to one another.

🌐 Plate Tectonics → lithospheric plates move over the asthenosphere.

🔴 Endogenic → forces originate inside Earth.

🔵 Exogenic → forces act from outside Earth.

⛰️ Folding → rocks bend under compression.

🪨 Faulting → rocks fracture and become displaced.

🌡️ Weathering → rocks break down in place.

🌊 Erosion → materials are moved from one place to another.

📦 Deposition → transported materials accumulate.

⬇️ Mass wasting → materials move downslope mainly because of gravity.

title: ⭐ UNIT 1 QUICK REVISION
notes:

🧭 Wegener → proposed Continental Drift Theory in 1912.

🧩 Evidence → coastline fit + rocks + fossils + paleoclimate.

🌐 Lithosphere → divided into moving plates.

🌊 Asthenosphere → ductile layer beneath lithosphere.

🔄 Plate boundaries → convergent + divergent + transform.

💥 Convergent → plates meet; subduction or collision.

🌊 Divergent → plates separate; new crust can form.

↔️ Transform → plates slide past; crust is neither created nor destroyed.

🔥 Convection → important mechanism associated with plate movement.

🔴 Endogenic → folding + faulting + earthquakes + volcanism.

🔵 Exogenic → weathering + erosion + deposition + mass wasting.

⛰️ Fold mountains → young and old.

🪨 Fault landforms → rift valley/graben + horst/block mountain.

🌎 Earthquake → sudden ground shaking caused by rock movement.

📡 Focus → earthquake origin; Epicenter → surface point above focus.

🌋 Volcano → opening/structure through which magma, gases and ash erupt.

🕳️ Intrusive landforms → batholith + sill + dyke.

💧 Weathering → physical + chemical.

🏞️ River landforms → V-shaped valley + gorge + waterfall + meander + ox-bow lake + flood plain + delta.

💨 Wind → sand dunes + barkhan + loess.

🌊 Sea → beach + spit + lagoon.

⬇️ Mass wasting → downslope movement under gravity.
